blocks.text: The closing notice about Jehoiachin describes more than a release from prison: he receives an ongoing daily allowance and eats at the Babylonian king’s table. Administrative tablets from Nebuchadnezzar’s palace record food or oil allocations to a ruler identified as Jehoiachin, king of Judah, along with his dependents and other Judeans. These records provide near-contemporary context for his continued recognition and palace support in Babylon, though they do not independently confirm the particular release scene described here.

The chapter’s sweep distinguishes Jehoiachin’s earlier removal with selected groups from the later fall of Jerusalem under Zedekiah and the further deportations listed in verses 28–30. Reading these episodes as a sequence helps prevent the Babylonian exile from being treated as one single, undifferentiated departure.

Jeremiah is a varied book, bringing together poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, restoration collections, oracles against nations, and a concluding appendix. A practical outline places chapter 52 after the nation oracles of chapters 46–51; this arrangement describes the received book without settling how its materials were composed.
